summary: Defines managed objects that provide an inverted mapping of the interface stack table, which records how network interface layers sit on top of each other. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Network layers sit like blocks in a tower. A normal list tells you what is above each block, and this one tells you what is below.

questions: what is the interface stack table
how to find interfaces above an interface in snmp
subtitle: A read-only upside-down copy of the interface stack table, so a manager can find what runs on top of an interface without reading everything.

tldr.problem: The ifStackTable is indexed with the higher-layer interface first, so finding which interfaces run on top of a given interface means reading the whole table, which is inefficient on devices with many interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The IF-INVERTED-STACK-MIB adds ifInvStackTable, which holds the same relationships with the lower-layer ifIndex first and the higher-layer ifIndex second.
tldr.outcome: A management application can read a small slice of the new table to see which interfaces sit above a particular interface. It adds no new information and is read-only.

today: RFC 2864 is a Proposed Standard with no recorded obsoleting or updating RFC. It extends the Interfaces Group MIB defined in RFC 2863.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2864 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. In particular it describes managed objects that give an inverted mapping of the interface stack table used to manage network interfaces.

The module is compliant to SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced by translation, and the result must be semantically equivalent except where objects are omitted because no translation is possible.
sections.eli5: This memo adds one extra list to the network manager's toolbox. The list tells the same story as an existing one, but from the other end.

sections.title: Interface Sub-Layers and the ifStackTable
sections.content:
MIB-II defines the generic 'interfaces' group for managing network interfaces. Experience with media-specific extensions showed a need to distinguish the multiple sub-layers beneath the internetwork layer. The RFC's example is an interface with PPP running over an HDLC link which uses a RS232-like connector, each with its own media-specific MIB module.

The IF-MIB (RFC 2863) meets this need by giving each sub-layer its own conceptual row in the ifTable. It also defines the ifStackTable, whose rows each record that a higher-layer interface runs on top of a lower-layer one, using ifIndex values as pointers to rows of the ifTable.
sections.eli5: A network connection is built in layers, like a stack of pancakes. Each layer gets its own line in a big table, and a second table says which pancake sits on which.

sections.title: The Inverted Table
sections.content:
The ifStackTable is indexed by the ifIndex values of the two interfaces, and the IF-MIB put the higher-layer interface first and the lower-layer second. A management application can therefore read a subset of it to find the interfaces underneath a particular interface. To find the interfaces on top, it has no alternative but to read the whole table, which is very inefficient on a device with many interfaces and many rows.

The ifInvStackTable has the same information with the INDEX order reversed: lower-layer interface first, higher-layer second. It has exactly the same number of rows as the ifStackTable, but in a different order, so reading a slice of it shows what runs on top of a particular interface.

For every ifIndex value z that identifies an active interface, at least two rows exist. For an interface with nothing stacked above or below it, they are ifInvStackStatus.z.0 and ifInvStackStatus.0.z, both active.
sections.eli5: The first list is sorted by the top block, so finding what is under a block is quick. The new list is sorted by the bottom block, so finding what is on top is quick too.

sections.title: The ifInvStackStatus Object
sections.content:
The only object is ifInvStackStatus, of type RowStatus, with MAX-ACCESS read-only. An instance exists for each instance of ifStackStatus and vice versa. If ifStackStatus.H.L exists then ifInvStackStatus.L.H must also exist, and the two always have the same value.

Unlike ifStackStatus, it cannot be written. To change a relationship between sub-layers H and L, an application must modify ifStackStatus.H.L, and the change is then reflected in the inverted table.

The module is IF-INVERTED-STACK-MIB, registered as mib-2 77.
sections.eli5: You can only look at the new list, not edit it. To change something you edit the original list, and the new one updates itself.

sections.title: Compliance Requirements
sections.content: The module's compliance statement, ifInvCompliance, covers SNMP entities that provide inverted information on the layering of network interfaces. It makes the group ifInvStackGroup mandatory. For ifInvStackStatus, support is only required for active. It also requires the ifStackGroup2 group from the IF-MIB.
sections.eli5: A device that wants to claim it supports this list must show the 'active' entries and must also keep the original list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
No object in this MIB has a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create. If it is implemented correctly, an intruder cannot alter or create its objects through direct SNMP SET operations.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and there is no control over who on even a secure network may GET or SET objects. The RFC recommends implementers consider SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). It is then the responsibility of the customer or user to configure the SNMP entity to give access only to principals with legitimate rights.
sections.eli5: Nobody can change this list by sending it a command. But anyone who can look at it should be someone you trust, so lock the door properly.
